ev.may_fc_tzolkin.offering.ok: Copal smoked on the stone altar; the priest tossed a handful of cacao beans into the fire and chanted a prayer. "The wind will settle," he promised.
ev.may_fc_tzolkin.wind: Let the child grow up windy
ev.may_fc_tzolkin.wind.ok: "Wind it is, then," the household decided. The priest shrugged and wrote your day into his book.
ev.may_fc_tzolkin.title: The sign of your day
ev.may_fc_tzolkin.text: The priest, the keeper of days, unfolded a screenfold book of bark paper and ran his finger along the rows of signs for a long time. You were born on a day Ik', the day of wind: such people, he says, are restless and quick to set off, but their fate is unsteady, like a flame in the wind. The sign can be strengthened with an offering of copal and cacao to the gods — or accepted as it is.
ev.may_fc_tzolkin.note: The sacred calendar, the tzolk'in, has 260 days: 20 day signs combined with the numbers 1 to 13. The Maya believed the sign of one's birthday shaped a person's nature and fate, and priests — "keepers of days" — interpreted the signs. Books were written on long strips of fig-bark paper coated with lime and folded like a screen.
ev.may_fc_tzolkin_keeper.title: The day-keeper's pupil
ev.may_fc_tzolkin_keeper.text: The old keeper of days who once strengthened your sign called you to him: "The wind in you has settled — so you can learn to listen." Now in the evenings you learn to count the days around the circle of two hundred and sixty, and to remember which sign bodes well and which ill.
ev.may_fc_tzolkin_road.title: The wind calls
ev.may_fc_tzolkin_road.text: When the porters of long-distance traders passed through your town, you begged to go with them as far as the next kingdom. For five days you carried a bundle of salt along forest trails and came back with a handful of cacao beans and a heap of stories. "Day of wind," was all the old priest said.
ev.may_fc_head.bind.ok: The boards were tied tightly to your head, and for some months you slept in a cradle like a little litter. Every morning grandmother admired you: "{g:Handsome as the young maize god|Lovely as the moon goddess}."
ev.may_fc_head.none.ok: Your mother put the boards aside: "Let the child grow the way it was born." Grandmother sulked for a week.
ev.may_fc_head.title: Boards for the head
ev.may_fc_head.text: Grandmother has brought two smooth boards and strips of cotton cloth: while the bones are soft, a baby's head is bound so that the brow grows high and sloping, like the maize god's. Almost everyone does it — nobles and commoners alike. Your mother hesitates: you cry at night as it is.
ev.may_fc_head.note: Like many peoples of Mesoamerica, the Maya reshaped their children's heads: while the bones were soft, a baby's head was bound with boards or bands. A long sloping brow recalled the head of the maize god and was thought beautiful; such skulls are found among people of every rank. According to Bishop Landa (16th century), a slight squint was also admired.
ev.may_fc_head_beauty.title: A brow like the maize god's
ev.may_fc_head_beauty.text: At the maize god's festival everyone's eyes were on you: that high sloping brow, that clean profile — fit to be carved on a stela. Grandmother, very old now, was beaming: "I was right to insist back then."
ev.may_fc_head_round.title: Round head
ev.may_fc_head_round.text: The other children called you "pumpkin" — your head is round, not like everyone else's. First you cried, then you fought, and then you outran your tormentors all the way to the temple — and the teasing stopped. Since then you have known for certain: the shape of your head is not what matters.
